classification.difficultyReason: Select the right-angle, straight-angle or revolution total and add or subtract the displayed sectors, identifying the reflex region where requested. Each part directly applies one taught angle relationship.

questions.mappingNote: Every part asks for an unknown angle with a reason: a,d,i use a straight angle; b uses a right angle; c,f add adjacent angles; e identifies a straight angle; g,h,j,k,l use a revolution. These directly assess unknown-angles-point.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–3 form an equation using adjacent angles, a revolution or a straight angle, then calculate the unknown. The geometric-arguments box gives totals of 90 degrees for a right angle, 180 degrees for a straight angle and 360 degrees for a revolution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply adjacent-angle, straight-angle and revolution totals to the supplied diagrams, giving reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify opposite rays at an intersection and name the vertically opposite angle, including intersections within larger figures.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess identifying a vertically opposite angle and expressing its name with Q as the middle letter; no angle calculation is required.
questions.methodNote: The geometric-arguments summary states that vertically opposite angles are equal. Example 4 identifies opposite angle sectors at intersecting straight lines using their vertex labels.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify opposite rays at an intersection and name the vertically opposite angle, including intersections within larger figures.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify and name the unmarked pair of alternate interior angles.

questions.mappingNote: The response asks for the second alternate interior pair after AEF and EFD are marked.
questions.methodNote: Identify alternate angles as interior angles on opposite sides of a transversal; name each angle with its vertex in the middle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify and name the unmarked pair of alternate interior angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify and name the unmarked interior angle pair on the same side of a transversal.

questions.mappingNote: The unnumbered prompt asks for the second co-interior pair, excluding the marked right-hand pair.
questions.methodNote: Identify angles between the two lines and on the same side of the transversal; name each angle with its vertex letter in the middle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify and name the unmarked interior angle pair on the same side of a transversal.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify whether each marked pair is corresponding, alternate or co-interior, then copy the given value or subtract it from 180 degrees and name the parallel lines.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses supplementary co-interior angles, b uses equal alternate angles, and c uses equal corresponding angles; finding unknown parallel-line angles is directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Corresponding and alternate angles are equal; co-interior angles sum to 180 degrees. State the angle relationship and the relevant parallel lines, following Examples 5–7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the appropriate parallel-line angle relationship and give a reason naming the parallel lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Plan several linked deductions without named intermediate unknowns: transfer angles along the marked parallel lines, combine or supplement sectors, and select the straight-angle or revolution total that isolates the marked angle.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts require unknown angles involving parallel lines. Part a uses co-interior angles and a revolution; b uses corresponding angles and a straight angle; c uses vertically opposite and co-interior angles; d uses alternate angles and a revolution.
questions.methodNote: Use corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles with the named parallel lines, followed by straight-angle or revolution facts. Give a reason for each step.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle properties with angles on a straight line or around a point.

classification.difficultyReason: First establish parallel lines using an angle-property converse, then use parallel-line angle properties to find an unknown.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the corresponding-angle converse followed by corresponding angles; parts b and c use the alternate-angle converse followed by alternate angles; part d uses supplementary co-interior right angles followed by supplementary co-interior angles on BD.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 gives the corresponding-angle, alternate-angle and co-interior-angle converses for proving parallelism; Examples 11–13 demonstrate reasons. Pages 7–8 demonstrate finding unknown angles using established parallel lines and naming the angle relationship and relevant parallel lines. Page 2 supplies right-angle and straight-angle facts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: First establish parallel lines using an angle-property converse, then use parallel-line angle properties to find an unknown.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a third interior angle directly from two given angles using the triangle angle sum.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–e supplies two interior angles and directly assesses subtracting their sum from 180 degrees; angle-sum-triangle is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 establishes that the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees. Page 19, Example 14, forms an angle-sum equation and calculates the remaining interior angle. Pages 2–3 establish angle notation and reasoned angle calculations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a third interior angle directly from two given angles using the triangle angle sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the triangle angle sum or exterior-angle theorem, express the relationship as a linear equation, and collect terms and solve. The hardest part first transfers a vertically opposite angle before forming the equation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b, c and f use the triangle angle sum; d, e and h use the exterior-angle theorem; g first uses vertically opposite angles and then the triangle angle sum. All parts also require solving a linear equation. General prerequisite algebra teaching is absent from the supplied evidence.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish straight, right and vertically opposite angles. Pages 18–19 establish triangle angle sums and the exterior-angle theorem, with Examples 14–15. Page 12 Example 10 demonstrates collecting angle terms and dividing to solve a geometric equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form and solve equations using triangle angle sums, exterior angles and vertically opposite angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose an order for linked deductions using marked parallel lines, straight or vertically opposite angles, and triangle sums. The harder diagrams require recovering an intermediate angle and carrying it into another triangle or parallel-line relationship, with no new construction needed.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts combine previously taught angle properties with triangle angle sums. Parts a, b, c and d use alternate/co-interior angles before triangle sums; e also uses a straight angle; f and h use intersecting lines; g uses the marked right angle.
questions.methodNote: Use straight angles and vertically opposite angles as in Examples 3–4; identify alternate or co-interior angles and name the parallel lines as in Examples 5–8; set up the triangle angle sum as in Example 14. Give a reason for each deduction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine parallel-line angle properties, angles at a point and triangle angle sums, giving reasons for several unknowns.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest parts require selecting successive triangles or inferring parallel lines from perpendiculars, then linking parallel-line, straight-angle and triangle-sum facts while giving reasons.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires a triangle angle sum or exterior angle together with earlier angle properties. Part a uses APQ then corresponding angles; b uses corresponding angles then VPQ; c uses two exterior angles; d uses RAP then AVB; e uses parallel and straight angles then ABV; f uses co-interior angles then an exterior angle; g uses perpendicular lines, co-interior and straight angles then ABV; h uses both triangle sums and adjacent straight angles.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 demonstrate adjacent and straight angles with named reasons. Pages 7–8 use corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles, naming the parallel lines. Pages 18–19 prove and apply triangle angle sums and exterior angles; Examples 14–15 show equations followed by the unknown angle and a reason.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Eight multistep diagrams combine triangle angle sums with parallel-line properties, straight angles and exterior angles, requiring reasons.

classification.difficultyReason: Part f requires identifying equal base angles in the whole isosceles triangle and transferring them into two right triangles to calculate the split apex angles.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b, d and e combine equal base angles with the triangle angle sum; c uses equal base angles and an exterior angle; f applies the angle sum separately to the two right triangles and transfers the equal base angles.
questions.methodNote: Use equal base angles of isosceles triangles, the 180-degree triangle angle sum, the exterior-angle theorem and right angles. Give geometric reasons as in Examples 14–18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines equal base angles with triangle angle sums, exterior angles and right angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate missing angles where necessary, then use equal angles to identify equal sides.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task combines missing-angle calculations with equal-side identification; unknown-sides-angles-figures is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use straight angles, the triangle angle sum and the exterior-angle theorem, then apply the converse of the isosceles base-angle property. Pages 23–24 explicitly state that equal angles have equal opposite sides; page 25 Example 17 models this inference.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate missing angles where necessary, then use equal angles to identify equal sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct labelled diagrams from prose and combine isosceles properties with angle calculations.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess missing angles from isosceles properties in student-constructed figures.
questions.methodNote: Part a uses straight angles and equal base angles. Part b follows page 25 Example 16: equal radii form an isosceles triangle, whose equal base angles are calculated using the triangle angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct labelled diagrams from prose and combine isosceles properties with angle calculations.

classification.difficultyReason: Students combine straight-angle and triangle sums, then reverse the isosceles property to infer equal opposite sides; part b also requires moving between the whole triangle and a smaller triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b use triangle angle sums and isosceles base angles; c–e infer equal sides from equal angles; f combines straight angles, a triangle angle sum and equal opposite sides.
questions.methodNote: Use straight-angle sums, triangle angle sums, equal base angles of isosceles triangles and the converse that equal angles have equal opposite sides. Page 25 Examples 17–18 illustrate equal opposite sides and exterior-angle reasoning.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine triangle angle sums, equal angles and opposite equal sides, with straight-angle reasoning.

classification.difficultyReason: Each diagram directly supplies the four quadrilateral angles or right-angle markers; part a requires collecting two equal unknown angles and dividing the remaining angle total by two.

questions.mappingNote: All five parts directly assess the quadrilateral angle sum. Part a additionally collects two occurrences of alpha and divides by two; b and c subtract three known angles; d and e interpret the supplied right-angle markers as 90 degrees.
questions.methodNote: Pages 27–28 define quadrilaterals and establish their 360-degree interior-angle sum. Example 19 on page 29 forms an angle-sum equation and simplifies it to find the unknown.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the quadrilateral angle sum, including two equal unknown angles in part a and supplied right angles in parts d and e.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate missing angles and sketch suitable quadrilaterals, including a non-convex quadrilateral.

questions.mappingNote: Each part applies the quadrilateral angle sum and asks for a sketch; part d additionally requires the non-convex case explicitly taught in this section.
questions.methodNote: Page 28 establishes the 360-degree quadrilateral angle sum. Page 29 Example 19 subtracts the known angles from 360 degrees. Pages 27 and 29 distinguish convex quadrilaterals from quadrilaterals with a reflex interior angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate missing angles and sketch suitable quadrilaterals, including a non-convex quadrilateral.

classification.difficultyReason: Part c requires recognising that the two isosceles triangles determine the sum of two individually unknown angles, introducing separate angle variables and combining them through the quadrilateral sum without finding either separately.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c combine equal-side triangle properties with angle sums; b uses common perpendiculars and parallel-line angles; d forms a quadrilateral equation; f combines triangle and quadrilateral sums. Part e requires clarification before its method can be verified.
questions.methodNote: Use straight angles, triangle and quadrilateral angle sums, equal base angles of isosceles triangles, and co-interior angles on parallel lines. Page 29 demonstrates forming an equation from a quadrilateral angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines several angle relationships, equal-side properties and multi-step deductions.

classification.difficultyReason: Students interpret the floor plan, establish parallel boundaries from right angles, transfer the wall angle to the table corner, and then use equal base angles and the triangle sum.

questions.mappingNote: Part a combines a marked right angle with equal base angles and the triangle angle sum. Part b combines parallel-line angle reasoning with equal base angles and the triangle angle sum. The shared geometric application is best classified as unknown-sides-angles-figures.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 demonstrate right-angle subtraction and straight-angle reasoning. Pages 7–8 establish corresponding and co-interior angles on parallel lines. Pages 23–24 state equal base angles in isosceles triangles and use the triangle angle sum; page 25 Example 16 applies these properties to calculate equal base angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine right-angle givens, parallel horizontal boundaries and equal base angles to evaluate angles in two isosceles triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Find each complementary angle by subtracting a given acute angle from 90 degrees.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses complementary angle pairs, so angle-pairs-point is the closest catalogue skill. Original teaching evidence defining 'complement' remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 Example 1 finds an unknown angle within a right angle using the sum of adjacent angles. Pages 2–3 support subtraction from a known angle total, but do not explicitly define complementary angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find each complementary angle by subtracting a given acute angle from 90 degrees.

classification.difficultyReason: Find each supplementary angle by subtracting the given angle from 180°.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses supplementary angle pairs, so angle-pairs-point is the closest catalogue skill. The subtraction method matches Example 3, but original prerequisite evidence defining supplementary angles remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states that angles in a straight angle sum to 180°. Page 3 Example 3 subtracts a known angle from 180° to find the remaining angle. Neither inspected page explicitly defines the term supplement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find each supplementary angle by subtracting the given angle from 180°.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest part requires recognising two isosceles triangles from equal half-diagonals and linking their angle sums through a straight angle, without assuming right angles at the corners.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses straight angles and the exterior-angle theorem; b uses crossing angles and triangle sums; c uses equal base angles and a linear equation; d uses isosceles triangles formed by the four equal half-diagonals, without assuming corner right angles; e uses the quadrilateral angle sum and a linear equation; f uses a revolution and the marked pairs of parallel sides. Original general prerequisite algebra evidence is missing for c and e.
questions.methodNote: Use straight and vertically opposite angles, triangle angle sums and exterior angles, equal base angles in isosceles triangles, quadrilateral angle sums and co-interior angles. Retain geometric equations followed by separate algebraic steps.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine angle sums, exterior angles, equal-sided triangles and parallel-line properties across six figures.

classification.difficultyReason: Part c requires selecting overlapping triangles, finding the full isosceles vertex angle and a smaller triangle angle, then subtracting to isolate the requested angle.

questions.mappingNote: The three parts combine parallel-line and triangle properties; part c assesses an isosceles triangle within an intersecting figure.
questions.methodNote: Name the relevant angle property, use triangle angle sums and equal base angles, and state reasons for intermediate angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines parallel-line, triangle and intersecting-line properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires an explanation linking a reflex angle to the triangle angle sum.

questions.mappingNote: Direct conceptual application of the triangle angle-sum theorem.
questions.methodNote: The interior angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires an explanation linking a reflex angle to the triangle angle sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Part b links an exterior angle to two equal base angles, then uses a right-triangle angle sum and a supplementary angle; the other parts use shorter familiar chains.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the triangle sum directly; b combines exterior and right-triangle angles; c combines parallel lines and an exterior angle.
questions.methodNote: Use triangle angle sums, the exterior-angle theorem, alternate angles and straight-angle sums, giving reasons.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires triangle angle sums together with exterior, parallel-line and right-angle relationships.

classification.difficultyReason: Several angle relationships must be connected across a zigzag with parallel end segments.

questions.mappingNote: The parallel end segments permit auxiliary parallel lines through the bends; pages 7–8 provide the relevant angle properties and multistep reasoning.
questions.methodNote: Use adjacent and supplementary angles, then transfer angles between parallel lines using corresponding or alternate angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Several angle relationships must be connected across a zigzag with parallel end segments.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must introduce auxiliary parallels through the bends and combine transferred angles symbolically. The numerical and matching symbolic diagrams scaffold the final configuration, which also requires a supplementary angle.

questions.mappingNote: Part a is a numerical parallel-line problem. Parts b–c generalise the same construction to symbolic angles; original teaching evidence for symbolic manipulation is missing.
questions.methodNote: Introduce auxiliary parallel lines, transfer corresponding or alternate angles, and add or subtract adjacent angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The same parallel-line construction is applied numerically and then to symbolic angle expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Students must add the missing radius, split the unknown vertex angle into two components, use equal radii to obtain two isosceles triangles, and combine symbolic angle sums around the centre to eliminate the components.

questions.mappingNote: Page 23 explicitly constructs isosceles triangles from radii; page 25 Example 16 applies this method. Pages 18–19 establish triangle angle sums, and page 2 supplies the revolution sum. No circle-angle theorem is assumed.
questions.methodNote: Use equal radii to form isosceles triangles, equal base angles, triangle angle sums and angles around a point.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires an auxiliary radius and a symbolic argument using two isosceles triangles and angles around the centre.

classification.difficultyReason: The task extends taught triangulation to polygons with concave corners, requiring valid internal subdivisions, then generalises the triangle counts into a relationship between side count and angle sum.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 18–19 establish the triangle angle sum. Page 28 explicitly derives the quadrilateral sum by dividing convex or concave quadrilaterals into triangles. Question 4 extends that method rather than supplying the polygon formula as the starting method.
questions.methodNote: Divide each polygon into triangles using internal diagonals and add their angle sums before generalising.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derives polygon angle sums from triangulation, including concave polygons, and generalises the relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Connects two isosceles triangles through a supplementary angle and their shared apex angle without a supplied diagram.

questions.mappingNote: The task combines the equal base angles of ADE with the equal base angles of ABC through their shared apex angle, directly assessing unknown angles in related figures.
questions.methodNote: Use angles on a straight line, equal base angles opposite equal sides, and the triangle angle sum. Pages 23–25 establish the isosceles properties; pages 18–19 establish the triangle angle sum; page 2 supplies straight-angle reasoning.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connects two isosceles triangles through a supplementary angle and their shared apex angle without a supplied diagram.

classification.difficultyReason: Constructs two configurations and combines square, equilateral and isosceles triangle properties to justify both possible angles.

questions.mappingNote: The task combines these taught properties in two configurations of a square and an equilateral triangle; finding unknown angles in figures is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use adjacent angles and angles in a revolution from page 2, the triangle angle sum from pages 18–19, and equal base angles and 60-degree equilateral angles from pages 23–25. Page 25 models concise angle calculations with geometric reasons.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs two configurations and combines square, equilateral and isosceles triangle properties to justify both possible angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalises the three exterior angles without numerical givens using straight angles and the triangle angle sum.

questions.mappingNote: Each labelled angle is supplementary to one interior angle. Summing these three relationships and using the triangle angle sum gives the requested total.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states that angles in a straight angle add to 180°. Pages 18–19 establish the triangle interior angle sum and define exterior angles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises the three exterior angles without numerical givens using straight angles and the triangle angle sum.
